title: "Consistent Hashing and Shard Ownership in Go"

# Consistent Hashing and Shard Ownership in Go

Hashing a key modulo the server count is easy, but changing that count remaps many keys. A consistent-hash ring assigns each node positions on a fixed hash space; a key belongs to its next clockwise position. Adding a node changes ownership mainly around the positions it acquires.

Use this for a cache-routing lab before attempting durable data migration. Routing a request and safely moving its data are separate operations.

## A deterministic ring

Save this complete example as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It uses SHA-256 truncated to 64 bits for stable routing, with 128 virtual positions per node. Virtual positions improve distribution; they do not guarantee equal load.

```go
package main

import (
	"crypto/sha256"
	"encoding/binary"
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

type point struct {
	hash uint64
	node string
}

type Ring []point

func hash(s string) uint64 {
	sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(s))
	return binary.BigEndian.Uint64(sum[:8])
}

func NewRing(nodes []string) Ring {
	var r Ring
	seen := make(map[string]bool)
	for _, node := range nodes {
		if seen[node] {
			continue
		}
		seen[node] = true
		for i := 0; i < 128; i++ {
			r = append(r, point{hash(fmt.Sprintf("%s/%d", node, i)), node})
		}
	}
	sort.Slice(r, func(i, j int) bool {
		if r[i].hash == r[j].hash {
			return r[i].node < r[j].node
		}
		return r[i].hash < r[j].hash
	})
	return r
}

func (r Ring) Owner(key string) (string, bool) {
	if len(r) == 0 {
		return "", false
	}
	h := hash(key)
	i := sort.Search(len(r), func(i int) bool { return r[i].hash >= h })
	if i == len(r) {
		i = 0
	}
	return r[i].node, true
}

func main() {
	old := NewRing([]string{"a", "b", "c"})
	next := NewRing([]string{"a", "b", "c", "d"})
	moved := 0
	for i := 0; i < 10000; i++ {
		key := fmt.Sprint(i)
		a, _ := old.Owner(key)
		b, _ := next.Owner(key)
		if a != b {
			moved++
			if b != "d" {
				panic("unexpected ownership change")
			}
		}
	}
	fmt.Println("keys moved to d:", moved)
}
```

The program prints a deterministic movement count. Compare it with `hash(key) % nodeCount` over the same keys. Measure per-node key counts and request counts separately: one key can dominate traffic.

Do not use a newly seeded `hash/maphash` function for cross-process ownership; its seed is process-local. All routers need identical hashing, node identifiers, virtual-position rules, and membership versions.

## Membership is configuration, not gossip by accident

Build each ring as an immutable snapshot. In a concurrent router, publish the new snapshot under an `RWMutex` or through `atomic.Pointer` to a wrapper. Never sort or append to a slice readers are traversing.

Assign every membership snapshot an epoch. A request carries the epoch it used; a node can reject stale ownership with a bounded retry response. When choosing replicas, walk clockwise until you find distinct physical nodes. Three virtual positions on one machine are one failure domain.

For durable storage, introduce migration states: copy the old owner's data, catch up writes, validate, switch the authoritative epoch, and retire the old copy after an explicit recovery window. Define who accepts writes during every state. Two owners accepting unrelated writes are a split-brain bug.

## Acceptance evidence

Test empty rings, duplicate node names, input-order independence, and stable routing across two processes. Add a node and verify that changed keys map only to that new node for the no-collision test fixture. Remove a node and verify that keys on surviving owners stay put. Inject a hot key and show why more virtual positions do not remove that bottleneck.

Continue in the [KV-store distribution exercise](../99-projects/99t-kv-http-store.qmd#distributed-store-design-extension). The Go code uses documented [SHA-256](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/sha256) and [binary encoding](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/binary) APIs; the ring and migration protocol are this book's lab design.
